_note: Medicines & Labs is Thuso Pharmacy: the formulary, interaction checks at prescribe and dispense, prescriptions through the §5.4 states, collections with a chain of custody (§10), the partner pharmacy's queue and lab orders whose results arrive on the lab-result door. Wave 2 contract; built in Wave 4 on packages/engines. The version ones the engine could not honestly answer are withdrawn, each naming its correction. Medicines keeps references and states, never a medicine, a dose or a result: packages/catalog/medicines.json#whereContentLives.

refusals.statement: The prescriber cannot verify their own script.
refusals.why: §5.4: separation of duties. Worked out from the references that acted, never the roles: the reference that prescribed is refused whatever role it verifies in.

refusals.statement: A driver never carries Schedule 5 or 6.
refusals.why: §10: controlled substances go nurse-only or with the patient present. Which schedules and which roles are packages/catalog/dispensing.json#schedules, and the schedule is the prescription's, never the carrier's to declare.

refusals.statement: A lab result is not complete until it is acknowledged.
refusals.why: Full Scope Engine 8.

refusals.statement: Nothing rewards taking a medicine.
refusals.why: Section 18A of the Medicines and Related Substances Act; held pending counsel, which is the founder's decision. No route offers a reward, so no route answers this: scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds rewards.json, the engine and every screen to it instead.

refusals.statement: Medicines holds no prescription by that reference.
refusals.why: A reference Medicines never issued is refused rather than acted on, so a mistyped reference cannot become a verification, a dispense or a collection of nothing.

refusals.statement: Only somebody the vetting register clears for this, today, may do it.
refusals.why: packages/catalog/vetting.json grants prescribe and dispense to roles, and Trust's events say whether the person or the pharmacy is verified today. A role the register does not grant, a person never heard verified, and one suspended or deactivated since, are each refused.

refusals.statement: This is done by a named person, and nobody was named.
refusals.why: Separation of duties, a patient's authorisation and a PIN's custody are arithmetic on who acted. A caller the runtime cannot name cannot be compared with anybody, so it is refused rather than treated as nobody in particular.

refusals.statement: That interaction check was not run for this patient at this stage.
refusals.why: A check at prescribe is not a check at dispense, and a check on one patient is not a check on another.

refusals.statement: That interaction check has already been cited.
refusals.why: One check stands behind one prescription or one dispense. A check cited twice is a second act that nobody checked.

refusals.statement: That check was not run. Say you have read why before you go on.
refusals.why: With no licensed source the check answers not checked, and a prescriber or a pharmacist who goes ahead does so knowing it, on the record, rather than reading an unrun check as a clean one.

secretRequestFields.why: The patient's hand-over PIN. The runtime keeps a digest of an accepted request's fields to refuse a reused key; a digest of six digits would be the six digits to anybody holding the store file, so the PIN is left out of it.

keptOnRefusal.why: A wrong PIN and a broken seal are refused, and a refusal rolls back everything else the handler did. The row that counts a wrong PIN and the row that voids a collection for a broken seal must survive that refusal, or the attempt limit never bites and a voided bag can be handed over on the next try.

response.why: The version in force. A change is made against it, and whatever starts now keeps it.

Each setting: its key, type, unit, the value in force and the version that set it, its default and provenance, its limits, who may change it, what a change reaches, its guardrail, and its clinical review.

The days of the week it covers, from the days packages/catalog/settings.json lists.
When it opens, as hours and minutes from 00:00.
When it closes, after it opens and no later than 24:00.

request.why: The new values, for a setting that is a list.
The new values, for a setting whose parts change together.
Why. Asked for by the handler rather than the binder, so that a change without one is refused in its own sentence rather than the general one for a missing field.
The settings version the admin was looking at. A change against an older one is refused.

response.why: When it took effect. Whatever started before it keeps the version it started under.

refusals.statement: Only the role a setting names changes it, and the change is recorded against a named person.
refusals.why: A setting decides how the platform treats people. The role or capability the setting names changes it, and a change is recorded against somebody who can be asked about it; everybody else only reads what is in force.

refusals.statement: There is no setting by that name.
refusals.why: An unknown setting is refused rather than stored, or the history fills with changes nothing reads.

refusals.statement: A change to a setting says why, or it is not made.
refusals.why: The history is read after something has gone wrong. A change with no reason is a number somebody moved.

refusals.statement: These settings changed after you opened them. Read what is in force now and decide against that.
refusals.why: Two admins changing one setting from screens opened at the same time would each overwrite a decision they never saw.

refusals.statement: That is not the kind of value this setting holds.
refusals.why: A word where a number belongs, or a list where one choice belongs, is a guess at what the admin meant, and a setting is never set by a guess.

refusals.statement: This setting is never nought or less, whatever its range says.
refusals.why: A wait of nothing, an offer that lapses as it is made and a fee of nothing are never what anybody meant. The range is a proposal and could be set wrongly; this refusal does not depend on it.

refusals.statement: Every role a setting names is a role on the vetting register.
refusals.why: A role the register does not hold is a gate nobody can be vetted through, which looks like a shortage rather than a mistake.

refusals.statement: That wording is longer than this setting allows.
refusals.why: The maximum is the space the words are read in. Wording that does not fit is cut off where somebody reads it.

refusals.statement: That wording drops a sentence this setting must always keep.
refusals.why: Some wording carries a promise that protects somebody. It may be reworded around that sentence and never without it.

refusals.statement: That rota leaves hours uncovered that must always have somebody on them.
refusals.why: A rota with a gap is an alert with nobody to go to, and nobody finds out until one arrives.

refusals.statement: That is outside what an admin may set for this setting.
refusals.why: The bounds, the allowed values and the allowed roles sit beside the default in the engine's contract. Moving a setting past them is a change to that contract, not a setting.

refusals.statement: That is already the value in force, so there is nothing to change.
refusals.why: A change that changes nothing is a row in the history saying something happened when nothing did.

refusals.statement: A hand-over PIN never works for longer than the collection it opens.
refusals.why: A PIN still working after its collection lapsed is a number that opens nothing honest and could be read out at the wrong door. Medicines' own rule between two of its settings, asked after the shared rules.

routes.emitsNoneBecause: No engine acts on a settings change. The engine that owns a setting reads the value in force when it starts something, and the event contract refuses an event nobody subscribes to. A change is the row it appends to the engine's own history, which the read route returns.
